extracted.intended_audience: educated lay readers, theologians and natural philosophers interested in anatomy and natural theology (early modern)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length natural theology argument that surveys anatomical structures (circulation, arteries, veins, glands, kidneys, breasts, seminal vessels, nerves) and adduces them as evidence of wise design by a Creator. The text enumerates numbered anatomical particulars and their functional explanations to persuade a sceptical reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blood circulation frequency and quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimates of pulses and blood volume showing the blood passes through the heart many times (e.g., 'whole Blood passes through the Heart 24 times in an Hour... 576 times in a Day and a Night'; other estimates giving 80–100 times per hour depending on ounces to the pound and pulse rate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue the extraordinary strength and endurance required of heart and vessels, implying deliberate design; numerical examples and alternative estimates (Lower, Dr. Lister) are given to show robustness of the phenomenon regardless of exact figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convictions from rapid blood motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The swiftness of the blood's motion, the strength of heart and arteries, and the countless branches of veins/arteries that carry it, together indicate design rather than chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages the reader (even an 'unhappy Atheist') to consider the continual, involuntary operation over decades as evidence of a 'powerful and gracious Ruler'; rhetorical exhortation rather than experimental protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orifices of lateral branches (alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that the orifices in veins and arteries are regularly positioned so blood passes appropriately into branches: 'Diſſect a Vein or an Artery Length-iſe, and obſerve how regularly the Orifices in both of them lie... through the latter, the Blood paſſes into the Branches that ſpring out of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References anatomical figures (Lower, Tab. III Fig. 6) as visual evidence; used to argue purpose/ends in the placement of orifices rather than accidental arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arteries grow narrower with distance from heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Arteries are larger near the heart and gradually narrower into many small branches; this gradation prevents blood from passing preferentially into lateral branches and ensures peripheral tissues receive nourishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains hydraulic reasoning: narrowing forces blood to press upon artery sides and enter lateral branches; uses the example of protuberances at orifices (Tab. III Fig. 6) to show adapted morphology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annular muscular fibres cause arterial contraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Arteries possess several tunics including annular fleshy fibres which contract when the artery is filled, narrowing the vessel and forcing blood forwards and sideways, maintaining circulation even while the heart is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes layered arterial structure (Tunics A, B, C, D, etc.) and functional role of annular fibres to prevent backflow and maintain flow; presented as evidence of 'an understanding Artificer'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inattention to pulse (insensibility) as designed
rubrics_metrics.description: Although arteries beat forcefully, healthy persons are normally insensible of the continual pulsation; this insensibility is presented as beneficial design so the mind's attention isn't constantly distracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against the explanation 'habit' as insufficient; contrasts perception of respiration with inability to feel pulse in health; mentions how disease/fear alter sensitivity as confirming design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrence (anastomosis) of veins and arteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent meeting of arteries with arteries and veins with veins, discharging into each other, provides alternative routes so if one vessel is disabled blood can pass another way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as protective redundancy/backup in circulatory design (benefit in case of amputation/obstruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of arteries into capillaries (vasa capillaria / vasa minima)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large arteries divide into an unspeakable number of very small tubes (capillaries) as they reach places requiring nourishment, allowing blood to slow and deposit nourishment to vessel walls and tissues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains necessity that fast-moving blood must pass through very narrow vessels to allow exchange; references Tab. III Fig. 4 and anatomical terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowness of tubes reduces blood speed (hydrostatic reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fluid propelled with the same force runs more slowly in narrow than in wide pipes because of adhesion/sticking to sides; illustrated by glass tube experiment (three tubes of different bore showing differing rise heights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a simple experimental demonstration with glass tubes EF G, tied threads, and qualitative hydrostatics to make the point accessible to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veins widen toward the heart (opposite gradient to arteries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Veins become larger as they approach the heart so that liquor passing from narrow to wider vessels runs more slowly; this prevents excessive swiftness in returning blood which would impede heart function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses simple bucket/pipe thought experiment and appeals to obvious mechanical principles to explain benefit of venous widening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valves in the veins prevent backflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Little valves in veins (sometimes one, sometimes two) stop blood when it attempts to go back and prevent weight of blood from pressing upon following parts, particularly important in veins carrying blood upwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasted with arteries which lack such valves; used as an adaptive feature placed 'where they are so serviceable, and not in the Arteries, where they would be prejudicial.' References Tab. IV Fig. 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential fibre strength in arteries vs veins
rubrics_metrics.description: Arteries (needing to force blood into narrow branches) have very strong muscular fibres; veins (growing larger where excessive swiftness would be harmful) have weaker/fewer fibres; exception: vena portae has stronger fibres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points to functional differentiation of vessel wall structure as evidence of purposeful adaptation; uses vena portae/liver example to explain exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of the blood (three principal functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three principal uses of the blood are: (1) separation of different humours (for bodily functions or discharge), (2) nourishment of the body, and (3) motion of the muscles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author restricts himself to a general account and avoids speculative details not yet well understood by learned men; purpose here is theological argument rather than physiological completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and distribution of humours (glands and organs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific humours are separated in many locations (lymph, gall in liver, juices in pancreas and glands, humours in stomach/intestines/eyes/nose/ears/mouth); the brain produces a spirituous humour conveyed by nerves to parts and exhaled by skin/respiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals to anatomical observations (e.g., Sanctorius on insensible perspiration) and to the adapted disposition of blood courses and glands as signs of design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kidney structure and urine passage (filtration and funneling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kidney filters saline watery humour through glandulous substance into tiny vessels that collect into papillae and a pelvis, then a ureter (funnel and pipe) to the bladder; bladder has muscles and a muscular valve to retain and expel urine voluntarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed morphological description (Tab. IV Fig. 3–4) used to show purposeful arrangement preventing backflow and corrosion (slimy inner coating) and providing controlled elimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bladder muscular valve and controlled evacuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bladder has strong muscular valve at its lower end preventing leakage until sufficient force causes expulsion; design ensures urine is not discharged continually and protects bladder lining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as functional evidence: ability to inflate bladder via ureter vs inability for wind to pass out same way; inner mucous coating to prevent corrosion by salty/sharp urine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the breasts for milk production and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Breast contains little glands where milk is separated from blood, little tubes where milk flows and is preserved until needed, terminating in the nipple for suckling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a focused example of adaptation for an important function (nourishment of offspring) and as an argument that such arrangement cannot be due to chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and route of seminal vessels and protective glands
rubrics_metrics.description: Spermatic arteries descend to testicles to bring seminal matter; veins and arteries are arranged so that on the left side the vein inserts into kidney vein rather than vena cava to avoid compression by arterial pulse; vas deferens carry seed to seminal vesicles where glands prevent leakage yet allow ejection; coverings (peritoneal tubes) prevent herniation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details of asymmetry and winding routes offered as evidence that the 'supreme Architect' may choose non-shortest paths for higher purposes; used to rebut simplistic claims that simplest path implies design absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convictions from aggregated anatomical particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregation of many anatomical particulars (veins, ureters, breasts, seminal vessels, vessels' courses and valves) jointly make it unreasonable to ascribe their arrangement to chance; even apparently non-simple routings may serve higher purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical synthesis urging the reader to inspect particulars and conclude design; acknowledges whole volumes exist on these specifics but presents the sampling as sufficient for conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of current physiological knowledge (humility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The precise mechanisms of nourishment and motion supplied by the blood are not fully known; author prefers silence to speculative guesses on unsettled physiological questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions the argument: some facts are incontestable and sufficient for theological inference, while other mechanistic details remain open to learned debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nerves and their branching as evidence of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Nerves form an innumerable concatenation of fine branches (like arteries for the blood) in which no branch, however small, is without use; damage to a nerve disables its muscle, showing nerves convey matter essential for motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invites readers to consult Willis and Vieussens for detailed figures (Tab. IV Fig. 6); uses the vital necessity of nerves for motion as further testimony to design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different opinions on the substance conveyed by nerves
rubrics_metrics.description: Antients recognized nerves as vessels conveying a certain matter from brain to muscles that is necessary for motion; cutting or obstructing a nerve renders the muscle immobile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes historical consensus as supporting the functional importance of nerves while avoiding committing to a specific modern theory.
